summary:
Same-sex conduct has been criminalised in Gambia since the colonial era. The Criminal Code adopted in March 2025 removed the 2014 provision permitting life imprisonment for "aggravated homosexuality" and instead sets a five-year minimum sentence for "unnatural offences", defined in the statute as any homosexual act, with no stated maximum penalty; "gross indecency" carries three years. Regional reporting on the 2025 package confirms the five-year minimum for homosexual acts. The offence attaches to conduct rather than to stated identity or expression.

Gender expression is separately restricted. Since 2013, section 167 of the Criminal Code forbids men to dress "as women", punishable by up to five years in jail or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi. A visitor presenting outside conventional male dress should expect this provision to be the most readily invoked against them. On 10 April 2012 a court remanded 18 men, 16 Senegalese, one Gambian and one Nigerian, arrested at a bar in the Tourism Development Area for "indecent practice" after police said they were wearing women's clothes; all charges were dropped on 1 August 2012.

The government of President Adama Barrow has not typically enforced these provisions. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report recorded no prosecutions under the statute while documenting significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons, and the 2020 report recorded arrests together with societal discrimination. The Barrow government has promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, while stating that there are no plans for liberalisation of the homosexuality laws.

Enforcement was broad under the previous long-term ruler, Yahya Jammeh. On 15 May 2008 he gave homosexuals 24 hours to leave the country and ordered the Inspector General of Police and the director of the Gambia Immigration Department to conduct mass patrols to "weed bad elements in society", warning that any hotel, lodge or motel lodging such individuals would be closed down. In June 2008 two Spanish men in their 50s, alleged to be gay, were arrested and detained at Kotu police station after taxi drivers reported them, and were released reportedly after the Spanish government intervened. On 23 December 2008 Frank Boers, a 79-year-old Dutch national, was arrested at Banjul International Airport when officials found him in possession of pornography including nude photos of himself and Gambian men; he was convicted of indecency and fined 100,000 dalasis in lieu of a two-year sentence. Arrests of gay people are believed to have been common during Jammeh's presidency, though data is lacking.

The 2014 Criminal Code (Amendment) Act defined "aggravated homosexuality" to include sexual acts with persons of the same gender under 18 years of age, carrying a mandatory life sentence, and imposed a mandatory life sentence specifically on gay or lesbian people living with HIV, a direct barrier to testing and treatment. In November 2014 state forces launched an investigation under that law producing at least eight arrests, including at least four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women. Detainees were held at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and allegedly tortured to compel confessions. Human Rights Watch's September 2015 report "State of Fear" documents arbitrary arrests, torture and killings under Jammeh, including his anti-gay rhetoric and explicit threats against LGBT people.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Gambia, and the country prohibits LGBTQ people from adopting children. No law or regulation protects residents against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and citizens cannot change their legal gender. In 2023 there were reports of healthcare workers refusing to honour LGBTQ+ people's privacy, which has negatively impacted HIV care for LGBTQ+ Gambians. No incidents of conversion therapy or of surgeries on intersex children or non-consenting adults were reported.

Societal hostility is documented at high levels. A 2021-2023 survey found 93% of Gambians would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. No LGBTQ+ organisations exist in the country after 2016 because it is considered too dangerous, children are raised within strict male and female gender norms with non-conformity treated as deviant and taboo, and the country's media promotes misinformation and harmful stereotypes toward LGBTQ+ people.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House rated Gambia "Partly Free" with 50/100 in Freedom in the World 2024, recording improved political freedoms under Barrow after 22 years of Jammeh's rule while listing severe discrimination against LGBT+ people among ongoing concerns. The improvement in political space has not been matched by decriminalisation or by statutory protection against discrimination.

The UK Home Office's country information and policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Gambia (v3.0, February 2023) assesses risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, and records country information on law and treatment. Its existence indicates that Gambia is treated by at least one foreign government as a country of origin where LGBT+ status carries well-documented risk.

The 2015 Human Rights Watch findings on arbitrary arrest, torture and killings concern the Jammeh enforcement climate rather than the current government, and the shift in enforcement practice since 2017 is the main variable in what a visitor should expect on the ground.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the March 2025 Criminal Code retained section 167's restriction on men dressing "as women" is not resolved in the available sources; the provision is sourced to the 2013 code and its current text is not confirmed.

The maximum penalty for "unnatural offences" under the 2025 code is not stated in any source reviewed, only the five-year minimum. Whether the 2025 code altered gender recognition, adoption or anti-discrimination provisions is not sourced.

Enforcement data under the Barrow government is thin: the 2021 US State Department report records no prosecutions, but no source covers 2022 to 2026 prosecution figures, and the claim that arrests were common under Jammeh is stated by sources as a belief for which data is lacking.

The UK Home Office policy note's current certification and internal-relocation conclusions are summarised at the level of scope only; its detailed country findings are not reproduced here.
